name: London
tagline: Imperial grandeur and restless reinvention along the Thames.
whenBlurb: Come late May through July for gardens, tennis and the racing calendar, or September for Frieze and fashion; skip the grey, wet depths of December to February.

ourTake.lede: London rewards depth over breadth, pick two neighbourhoods and live in them rather than sprinting between landmarks. The great museums are free and best in the first hour after opening; save the blockbuster shows for a members' hour. Skip the tourist afternoon teas on the strand and book a proper one at a hotel that has done it for a century.
ourTake.comeIf: You want theatre, tailoring, museums and the finest Indian food outside India.
ourTake.skipIf: You are on a tight budget or want reliable sunshine.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Claridge's
items.description: The city's grande dame, Art Deco poise that has anchored Mayfair for over a century.

items.name: The Connaught
items.description: Discreet, clubby and quietly grand, the address for those who prefer to be known, not seen.

items.name: The Savoy
items.description: Thames-side theatre and history, the London hotel everyone has heard of, and it earns the name.

items.name: The Peninsula London
items.description: The newest of the great houses, a Belgravia debut with the group's famous precision.

items.name: Raffles London at The OWO
items.description: The Old War Office reborn, Whitehall grandeur turned into a hotel of real gravity.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental Hyde Park, London
items.description: Park-facing and precise, the group's London flagship, steps from Harrods.

items.name: The Dorchester
items.description: Park Lane gold-leaf glamour, unapologetically grand, endlessly familiar.

items.name: The Berkeley
items.description: A rooftop pool over the rooftops of Knightsbridge, and a fashion-literate wit throughout.

items.name: The Lanesborough
items.description: Regency splendour and a butler on every floor, old-world London at full volume.

items.name: Bulgari Hotel London
items.description: Italian-jeweller cool below Hyde Park, the quiet, contemporary counterpoint to the grand dames.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel London at Park Lane
items.description: The surest hands on Park Lane, service you never have to think about.

items.name: 45 Park Lane, Dorchester Collection
items.description: The Dorchester's chic younger sibling, Art Deco lines and Hyde Park at the window.

items.name: The Emory
items.description: London's first all-suite hotel, the Maybourne group's most private new address.

items.name: The Ritz London
items.description: Louis XVI gilt and the most famous tea in the world, Edwardian London, immaculately kept.

items.name: Corinthia London
items.description: A vast, light-filled Victorian house between the river and Trafalgar Square.

items.name: Rosewood London
items.description: A Belle Époque courtyard house that feels like a private London residence.

items.name: The Langham, London
items.description: The original grand hotel of Europe, reborn, and still setting the standard for afternoon tea.

items.name: Hotel Café Royal
items.description: A landmark of old Regent Street, now a polished, design-led base at the heart of the West End.

items.name: Brown's Hotel, a Rocco Forte Hotel
items.description: London's oldest hotel, a warm, literary Mayfair townhouse of a place.

items.name: The Beaumont
items.description: An Art Deco jewel with the ease of a private club, small, and all the better for it.

items.name: The Cadogan, A Belmond Hotel
items.description: A Chelsea townhouse hotel with its own private garden square, rare, green and calm.

items.name: The Twenty Two
items.description: A members'-club-and-hotel in a Grosvenor Square mansion, the address of the moment.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental Mayfair, London
items.description: The group's newer Mayfair house, contemporary calm off Hanover Square.

items.name: The Chancery Rosewood
items.description: The old US Embassy on Grosvenor Square, reimagined as a grand all-suite house.

items.name: The Goring
items.description: The last great family-owned London hotel, and the Royal Family's own choice.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel London at Ten Trinity Square
items.description: A Beaux-Arts landmark by the Tower, grand City grandeur with Four Seasons ease.

items.name: Ham Yard Hotel, Firmdale Hotels
items.description: A hidden Soho urban village, bowling alley, roof garden and Firmdale colour.

items.name: Haymarket Hotel, Firmdale Hotels
items.description: A John Nash landmark with an indoor pool and Firmdale's fearless colour.

items.name: The Stafford London
items.description: A tucked-away St James's address with a famous American Bar and cobbled mews calm.

items.name: Pan Pacific London
items.description: A sleek, tall City house with one of the best hotel pools in London.

items.name: The Ned
items.description: A former bank turned all-day theatre, nine restaurants under a soaring banking hall.

items.name: The Kimpton Fitzroy London
items.description: A landmark Victorian palace on Russell Square, grand bones at a gentler price.

items.name: One Aldwych
items.description: A contemporary Edwardian house with a chlorine-free pool, in the thick of theatreland.

items.name: Great Scotland Yard Hotel
items.description: The old police headquarters, now a characterful hotel a whistle from Trafalgar Square.

items.name: The Mayfair Townhouse
items.description: A row of Georgian townhouses in the heart of Mayfair, polished and well-placed.

items.name: The Marylebone
items.description: A smart, contemporary base on Marylebone's village-like high street.

items.name: The Zetter Townhouse Marylebone
items.description: An eccentric, cocktail-loving townhouse with real personality.

items.name: Broadwick Soho
items.description: A joyful, maximalist Soho debut, colour, a rooftop bar and a sense of fun.

items.name: The Portrait by the National Portrait Gallery
items.description: A small hotel atop the National Portrait Gallery, with a rooftop over Trafalgar Square.

items.name: Covent Garden Hotel, Firmdale Hotels
items.description: Firmdale's English-country-house charm dropped into the middle of theatreland.

items.name: Tower of London
items.description: Nine centuries of royal palace, fortress and prison on the Thames, come for the Crown Jewels, the Yeoman Warder (Beefeater) tour and the ravens. Book the first timed slot to beat the crowds around the jewels.

items.name: Westminster Abbey
items.description: The coronation church of English and British monarchs since 1066, and burial place of kings, poets and scientists. The Poets' Corner and the high Gothic nave reward a slow, unhurried visit.

items.name: British Museum
items.description: London's most-visited attraction and a free walk through world civilisations, the Rosetta Stone, Parthenon sculptures and the Egyptian galleries. Vast, so pick two or three galleries rather than trying to see it all; the Great Court is a fine place to regroup.

items.name: St Paul's Cathedral
items.description: Wren's masterpiece with the second-largest cathedral dome in the world. Climb to the Whispering Gallery and on to the Golden Gallery for a City panorama, then find quiet in the crypt.

items.name: Buckingham Palace & Changing the Guard
items.description: The monarch's official residence; the free Changing of the Guard ceremony (most days in summer, alternate days off-season) is pure London pageantry. In summer, the State Rooms open for tours, worth booking ahead for the throne room and picture gallery.

items.name: National Gallery
items.description: Free, and one of the great European painting collections, Van Gogh's Sunflowers, Turner, Vermeer, Caravaggio, all in one loop off Trafalgar Square. An hour with a handful of rooms beats a rushed march.

items.name: Tate Modern
items.description: A former power station turned into the world's most-visited modern art gallery, with free collection displays and a top-floor viewing level over the river. Cross the Millennium Bridge from St Paul's for the classic approach.

items.name: Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A)
items.description: The world's largest museum of art and design, fashion, jewellery, sculpture, Islamic and South Asian galleries under one roof, free to enter. The Jameel Gallery of Islamic art and the cast courts are highlights; the garden café is a lovely pause.

items.name: Natural History Museum
items.description: A cathedral-like Victorian building holding 80 million specimens, Hope the blue whale skeleton soars over Hintze Hall, and the dinosaur gallery is a guaranteed hit with children. Free, and multi-generation friendly.

items.name: Houses of Parliament & Big Ben
items.description: The Palace of Westminster on the river, its Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben) freshly restored. UK and overseas visitors can tour the Commons and Lords, or simply photograph it from Westminster Bridge at dusk.

items.name: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew
items.description: A UNESCO-listed botanic garden with over 50,000 living plants, the vast Victorian Palm House and Temperate House, and a treetop walkway. A green, restful full morning, easy and pram-friendly for a multi-generational group.

items.name: Maritime Greenwich & Royal Observatory
items.description: Stand astride the Prime Meridian at the Royal Observatory, see the Cutty Sark tea clipper and the painted hall of the Old Royal Naval College, with a skyline view back to the City. Arrive by river boat for the best of it.

items.name: Borough Market
items.description: London's oldest food market (trading since 1756) with 100-plus stalls of cheese, charcuterie, produce and street food. Go mid-morning on a weekday for room to graze; plenty of veg-friendly options among the stalls.

items.name: The View from The Shard
items.description: The observation decks of western Europe's tallest building, 244m up, with a near-360 sweep taking in Tower Bridge, the river and, on a clear day, out to the hills. Time it for sunset; private and premium ticket options exist.

items.name: Sky Garden
items.description: A free, glass-domed public garden on top of the 'Walkie-Talkie' with 360-degree City views, book a timed slot in advance, or reserve a table at one of its restaurants for a guaranteed window seat.

items.name: Tower Bridge
items.description: London's most theatrical bridge; walk the high-level glass-floor walkway and see the Victorian steam engine rooms, or simply time a visit for a bascule lift (schedule published online). Best photographed from the South Bank.

items.name: Hyde Park & Kensington Gardens
items.description: Central London's great green lung, row or paddle on the Serpentine, walk to the Diana Memorial Fountain, or watch horses on Rotten Row. Speakers' Corner on a Sunday is a curiosity worth catching.

items.name: Regent's Park & Primrose Hill
items.description: Formal rose gardens (12,000-plus blooms in Queen Mary's Garden), an open-air theatre in summer, and the climb up Primrose Hill for one of the city's finest protected skyline views. Bring a picnic for the hill at golden hour.

items.name: Richmond Park
items.description: London's largest Royal Park, 2,500 acres of ancient oaks and free-roaming red and fallow deer, with the framed 'protected view' of St Paul's from King Henry's Mound. Feels like open countryside inside the city.

items.name: Hampstead Heath
items.description: Wild, hilly heathland with the famous view from Parliament Hill, swimming ponds, and Kenwood House, a Robert Adam villa with free-entry old masters, at its northern edge. A proper lungful of countryside twenty minutes from the centre.

items.name: Notting Hill & Portobello Road Market
items.description: Pastel townhouses and the mile-long Portobello Road antiques market (best on Saturdays). Wander the quiet crescents and mews, browse the vintage and antique dealers, then find brunch on Westbourne Grove.

items.name: Covent Garden
items.description: The restored market piazza with street performers under the glass roof, the Royal Opera House on the corner, and boutique-lined side streets. A natural base for a West End evening, theatre, dinner and people-watching.

items.name: West End Theatre
items.description: One of the two great English-language theatre capitals, long-running musicals like The Lion King and Les Misérables alongside new plays and star-led runs. Book premium seats ahead; a matinee suits a family day.

items.name: Royal Opera House
items.description: Home of The Royal Opera and The Royal Ballet in a lavish Covent Garden theatre. See a performance, or take a daytime backstage tour and have a drink on the Paul Hamlyn Hall terrace overlooking the piazza.

items.name: Wigmore Hall
items.description: London's most beloved recital hall, an intimate Arts-and-Crafts room celebrated for its acoustic and its chamber-music and song programme. For a connoisseur, an evening here is more rewarding than any big arena.

items.name: Ronnie Scott's Jazz Club
items.description: The legendary Soho jazz club, running since 1959, still the room where the great names play when in London. Book a table for the late set; small, dark and the real thing.

items.name: Thames river cruise to Greenwich
items.description: The best way to read the city, glide past Parliament, the Tate, Tower Bridge and Canary Wharf on an Uber Boat clipper down to Greenwich. A commentary sightseeing cruise or a private charter both work; UHNI groups can book a boat outright.

items.name: Little Venice & Regent's Canal walk
items.description: Painted narrowboats, willows and canalside cafés where two canals meet, with a towpath walk (or a canal boat) through Regent's Park and the zoo to Camden. A gentle, little-touristed slice of London.

items.name: South Bank & Thames Path walk
items.description: The riverside promenade from Westminster past the London Eye, Southbank Centre, National Theatre and Tate Modern to Tower Bridge, street food, book stalls and skyline the whole way. The single best free walk in the city.

items.name: The Wallace Collection
items.description: A free national museum in a Marylebone townhouse, Old Master paintings (Frans Hals' Laughing Cavalier), Sèvres porcelain, armour and gilt furniture, with a glass-roofed courtyard restaurant. An overlooked jewel a step off Oxford Street.

items.name: Sir John Soane's Museum
items.description: The house-museum of a great architect, left exactly as he arranged it, a labyrinth of antiquities, Hogarth's Rake's Progress and an Egyptian sarcophagus lit by hidden skylights. Free, small, and utterly singular; the candlelit evenings are magic.

items.name: Leighton House
items.description: A Victorian artist's fantasy home built around the Arab Hall, a domed courtyard glittering with antique Damascus tiles and a fountain. A jewel-box of a museum in leafy Holland Park.

items.name: Dennis Severs' House
items.description: A candlelit, immersive time capsule of a Georgian silk-weaver's house, experienced in silence as if the imaginary family has just left the room. Unlike anything else in London, book the atmospheric evening visit.

items.name: Fortnum & Mason
items.description: The royal grocer since 1707, the food hall of hampers, teas and preserves is a destination in itself, and afternoon tea in the Diamond Jubilee Tea Salon upstairs is a classic. Excellent for gifts to take home.

items.name: Afternoon tea at The Ritz
items.description: The quintessential London ritual, served in the gilded Palm Court to a live pianist since 1906. Dress code applies (jacket and tie for gentlemen); a memorable occasion for a special family lunch.

items.name: Harrods
items.description: The vast Knightsbridge department store, the food halls, the Egyptian escalator and every luxury house under one roof. Personal shopping and by-appointment services make it painless for serious buyers.

items.name: Liberty London
items.description: A mock-Tudor emporium built from old ships' timbers, famed for its printed fabrics, homeware and beauty hall, as much a piece of design history as a shop. The haberdashery and scarf rooms are a highlight.

items.name: Savile Row
items.description: The home of bespoke tailoring, where houses like Huntsman and Anderson & Sheppard have dressed the world for two centuries. Book a fitting for a made-to-measure suit, the London indulgence for the discerning gentleman.

items.name: Kensington Palace
items.description: A working royal residence set in Kensington Gardens, with the King's and Queen's State Apartments and rotating exhibitions of royal dress. Follow with tea at the Orangery in the gardens.

items.name: Columbia Road Flower Market
items.description: A single East End street erupting with cut flowers, plants and shrubs every Sunday, hemmed by independent shops and cafés. Go early for the colour and calm, later for the traders' end-of-day bargains.

items.name: Shoreditch & Brick Lane
items.description: East London at its most creative, street art, vintage stores, the Old Truman Brewery and one of the city's best concentrations of South Asian restaurants along Brick Lane. Sunday markets (UpMarket, Boiler House) are the day to come.

items.name: Camden Market & Camden Lock
items.description: A sprawling warren of over 1,000 stalls by the canal, food from every corner of the world, vintage, music history and eccentricity. Loud and young; ride a canal boat in from Little Venice to arrive well.

items.name: Coal Drops Yard, King's Cross
items.description: Reborn Victorian coal warehouses turned into a design-led shopping and dining quarter beside the canal, next to Granary Square's fountains. Smart, calm and thoroughly contemporary, a good antidote to the tourist crush.

items.name: Warner Bros. Studio Tour London – The Making of Harry Potter
items.description: The actual sets, costumes and props from all eight films, the Great Hall, Diagon Alley and the Hogwarts model. A 20-mile trip north of the city; tickets are timed and must be booked well ahead. A sure-fire family day.

items.name: Windsor Castle
items.description: The oldest and largest occupied castle in the world and a favourite royal residence, the State Apartments, St George's Chapel and a Changing of the Guard of its own. Under an hour by train from Paddington or Waterloo.

items.name: Oxford
items.description: The dreaming-spires university city, the Bodleian Library, Christ Church's great hall and quad, and a punt on the Cherwell. An hour by fast train from Paddington, walkable from the station.

items.name: Bath
items.description: A honey-stone Georgian city built around Roman baths and Jane Austen's world, the Roman Baths, the Royal Crescent and Bath Abbey, all on foot. About 90 minutes by train from Paddington.

items.name: Cambridge
items.description: The riverside university city, King's College Chapel, the colleges' hidden courts, and punting along the Backs past the great libraries. Under an hour by train from King's Cross.

items.name: Hampton Court Palace
items.description: Henry VIII's Tudor palace by the Thames, the great kitchens, the state apartments and the famous hedge maze in the formal gardens. Reachable by train from Waterloo, or grandly by river boat in summer.

items.name: Alain Ducasse at The Dorchester
items.description: One of the city's handful of three-stars, Ducasse's grand French, immaculately kept.

items.name: Sketch (Lecture Room & Library)
items.description: The pink room everyone photographs, and cooking serious enough for three stars.

items.name: CORE by Clare Smyth
items.description: Clare Smyth's ode to British produce, the first UK woman to hold three stars.

items.name: The Ledbury
items.description: Brett Graham's long-adored room, back at the very top after regaining its third star.

items.name: Gordon Ramsay Restaurant
items.description: Ramsay's Royal Hospital Road flagship, the longest-held three stars in the country.

items.name: Hélène Darroze at The Connaught
items.description: Darroze's warm, produce-led French, in one of Mayfair's most gracious rooms.

items.name: The Ritz Restaurant
items.description: Classical haute cuisine in a gilded Louis XVI room, the UK's most celebrated dining room.

items.name: Brooklands by Claude Bosi
items.description: Claude Bosi's rooftop room at The Peninsula, refined French with a view.

items.name: Ikoyi
credentials: World's 50 Best Restaurants No. 15 (2025, Highest Climber)
items.description: London's most exciting kitchen, sub-Saharan flavours and spice, reimagined at the highest level.

items.name: A. Wong
items.description: The only two-star Chinese restaurant in Europe, regional China, exactingly rendered.

items.name: Trivet
items.description: A wine-obsessed two-star from an ex-Fat Duck team, precise, and quietly brilliant.

items.name: Story
items.description: Tom Sellers' narrative tasting menu, playful, personal, and technically superb.

items.name: Kitchen Table
items.description: A counter for a handful of guests, cooked right in front of you, intimate and exact.

items.name: Da Terra
items.description: A Brazilian-Italian tasting menu with real heart, one of the East End's finest tables.

items.name: Alex Dilling at Hotel Café Royal
items.description: Gossamer-fine haute French cooking above Regent Street, a serious two-star.

items.name: Gymkhana
items.description: The colonial-club Indian room that raised the bar for the whole city, now two stars.

items.name: La Dame de Pic London
items.description: Anne-Sophie Pic's delicate, aromatic French, inside Ten Trinity Square.

items.name: Kol
items.description: Ex-Noma chef Santiago Lastra's Mexican, British ingredients, Mexican soul.

items.name: Endo at The Rotunda
items.description: A rooftop sushi counter of great purity, Endo Kazutoshi's London omakase.

items.name: Sushi Kanesaka
items.description: A jewel-box Ginza-style omakase inside 45 Park Lane, the quietest luxury in Mayfair.

items.name: The Araki
items.description: A tiny, revered sushi counter, one of the rarest seats in the city.

items.name: Dinner by Heston Blumenthal
items.description: Heston's history-of-British-food, staged over Hyde Park at the Mandarin Oriental.

items.name: Marcus at The Berkeley
items.description: Marcus Wareing's polished, produce-led room in one of Knightsbridge's grand hotels.

items.name: Mountain
items.description: Tomos Parry's live-fire follow-up to Brat, Basque-leaning, and one of the hottest tables in town.

items.name: The Clove Club
items.description: A long-running critical darling in Shoreditch Town Hall, modern British, quietly assured.

items.name: Trishna
items.description: Coastal south-west Indian cooking in a stylish Marylebone room, the sister to Gymkhana.

items.name: Benares
items.description: Boundary-pushing Indian on Berkeley Square, a Mayfair fixture that changed perceptions.

items.name: Veeraswamy
items.description: London's oldest Indian restaurant, open since 1926, and still holding its star.

items.name: Ambassadors Clubhouse
items.description: The UK's first Punjabi restaurant to hold a star, a JKS ode to undivided Punjab.

items.name: Kanishka
items.description: Atul Kochhar's celebration of India's lesser-known regional kitchens.

items.name: Amaya
items.description: Small Indian grill plates over open flame, light, sharing-led, and long-starred.

items.name: Pied à Terre
items.description: One of London's longest-standing starred rooms, refined French, quietly enduring.

items.name: Humble Chicken
items.description: Angelo Sato's yakitori, every part of the bird over charcoal, and a star to show for it.

items.name: Trinity
items.description: Adam Byatt's neighbourhood classic, the best table south of the river.

items.name: Bouchon Racine
items.description: Full-flavoured French bistro cooking above a pub, critically adored, and good value for it.

items.name: OMA
items.description: Greek and eastern-Med cooking over fire in Borough Market, the highest new entry of its year.

items.name: AngloThai
items.description: Thai cooking through a British-seasonal lens, buzzy, personal and very hard to book.

items.name: BiBi
items.description: Chet Sharma's inventive modern Indian, a Mayfair kitchen full of quiet ideas.

items.name: Chishuru
items.description: West African cooking from the first Black female chef to win a UK star.

items.name: Brat
items.description: Tomos Parry's original, whole turbot over fire, and a room that has never cooled.

items.name: Chez Bruce
items.description: A south-London institution, unshowy, French-leaning cooking of great consistency.

items.name: Akoko
items.description: A West African tasting menu of real refinement, spice and craft in equal measure.

items.name: The Cinnamon Club
items.description: Vivek Singh's elegant Indian in the old Westminster Library, a grand, landmark room.

items.name: Wildflowers
items.description: Mediterranean, live-fire cooking and warm personal service, SquareMeal's No. 1 London room.

items.name: The Devonshire
items.description: The most wanted pub in London, a perfect pint, an open fire and Guinness done properly.

items.name: St. JOHN
items.description: The nose-to-tail temple that reshaped British cooking, plain, honest and iconic.

items.name: Tamila
items.description: A fresh, modern take on South Indian, the chilli-cheese dosa has a following.

items.name: Brutto
credentials: The Good Food Guide, Best Local Restaurants 2025
items.description: A Florentine trattoria run with love, simple, generous, and always full.

items.name: Ida
credentials: The Good Food Guide, Best Local Restaurant in London 2025
items.description: A tiny family-run Italian doing the cooking of Le Marche, the neighbourhood's pride.

items.name: Cinder
credentials: The Good Food Guide, Best Local Restaurants 2025
items.description: Modern European cooking over live fire in a warm neighbourhood room.

items.name: Lorne
credentials: The Good Food Guide, Best Local Restaurants 2025
items.description: A small, wine-literate room doing precise modern-British plates.

items.name: Mambow
credentials: The Good Food Guide, Best Local Restaurants 2025
items.description: Punchy, homestyle Malaysian cooking with a devoted local following.

items.name: Chuku's
credentials: The Good Food Guide, Best Local Restaurants 2025
items.description: Nigerian tapas in a joyful, generous room, sharing, done the West African way.

items.name: Miga
credentials: The Good Food Guide, Best Local Restaurants 2025
items.description: Honest, homestyle Korean cooking in an easygoing neighbourhood setting.

items.name: Connaught Bar
items.description: The bar that redefined the hotel bar, twice the world's best, and still the finest martini in London, made at your table.

items.name: Scarfes Bar
items.description: A gentleman's-club snug of roaring fires, live jazz and Gerald Scarfe's caricatures, inside Rosewood London.

items.name: The American Bar at The Savoy
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars, long-standing multiple listee
items.description: The oldest surviving cocktail bar in Britain, the birthplace of drinks the whole world now orders.

items.name: Coburg Bar
credentials: A bar of international standing, inside a MICHELIN Three-Key hotel
items.description: The Connaught's quieter salon, a fireside library of a bar, for conversation over a considered old-fashioned.

items.name: Beaufort Bar at The Savoy
items.description: Black-and-gold Art Deco drama on the Savoy's old cabaret stage, theatrical drinks, live music.

items.name: Artesian
items.description: The four-times World's Best bar at The Langham, a grand room that still makes ambitious, beautiful drinks.

items.name: Tayēr + Elementary
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars 2025 (No. 5, highest in London)
items.description: Two bars in one, a relaxed front room and a chef's-table counter where the ingredients change by the day.

items.name: Satan's Whiskers
items.description: A cramped, cash-only East End room with taxidermy on the walls and some of the best drinks-making in the city.

items.name: Kwãnt
items.description: A subterranean Mayfair den of Erik Lorincz's cocktail omakase, precise, personal, quietly world-class.

items.name: A Bar with Shapes for a Name
items.description: Remy Savage's Bauhaus-minded room, a menu built on ideas, in an East London bar that thinks like a gallery.

items.name: Three Sheets
items.description: A tiny, brothers-run Soho bar doing classics with quiet modern precision, no theatre, just excellent drinks.

items.name: Lyaness
items.description: Ryan Chetiyawardana's riverside laboratory, bold, ingredient-driven cocktails few other bars would attempt.

items.name: Swift
items.description: A quick aperitivo upstairs, a candlelit whisky den below, two moods, both faultless.

items.name: Aqua Shard
credentials: A landmark high-rise bar in The Shard
items.description: Cocktails on the 31st floor of the tallest building in Western Europe, the whole city laid out beneath you.

items.name: Seabird
credentials: A landmark rooftop bar, atop the Hoxton Southwark
items.description: London's longest rooftop bar, oysters, a spritz and an open sweep across the Thames to St Paul's.

items.name: Radio Rooftop
credentials: A landmark rooftop bar, atop the ME London hotel
items.description: A glamorous perch above the Strand with the river and the city's skyline in one glance.

items.name: Nightjar
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars, former top-ten listee
items.description: A 1920s speakeasy of live jazz and elaborate cocktails, London after dark at its most romantic.

plan.heading: 4 days in London, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle in at Claridge's, then walk Green Park to Buckingham Palace and along the Mall.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Wallace Collection for the armour and the Fragonards, followed by tea back at Claridge's.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Alex Dilling at Hotel Café Royal, two Michelin stars and quietly precise.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The British Museum early, with a private guide through the Enlightenment and the Assyrian reliefs.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Courtauld at Somerset House for the Impressionists, then a slow walk along the Strand.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Ikoyi in St James's, West African-rooted and among the world's best.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Saatchi or a morning at the Chelsea Physic Garden, then the King's Road at ease.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A car to Kew Gardens for the Palm House and the Temperate House.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at The Ritz Restaurant, the finest dining room in London, jacket and tie.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Westminster Abbey before the crowds, then the Churchill War Rooms.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The National Gallery for an hour with the Van Eycks and the Turners.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: An evening at the Royal Opera House, supper afterwards at The Wolseley.

items.name: Mayfair
items.description: Galleries, grand hotels and the best tables, for classic, moneyed London.

items.name: Chelsea / Belgravia
items.description: Garden squares and quiet wealth, suits a residential, unhurried stay.

items.name: Marylebone
items.description: Village-like high street and townhouses, the most livable central address.

events.name: Wimbledon
events.note: The oldest tennis championship, and London's summer social centrepiece.

events.name: Frieze London
events.note: The contemporary art fair that turns Regent's Park and the whole city into a gallery.

events.name: Chelsea Flower Show
events.note: The RHS's flagship show and a fixture of the London season.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay in Mayfair for quiet proximity to Bond Street and the parks; better restaurants and members' clubs expect a jacket in the evening, and a table at the most sought-after rooms is arranged well ahead.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Heathrow (or London City for the closest run to Mayfair); a pre-booked chauffeur in an S-Class or Range Rover meets you airside and clears the terminal in minutes.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with a London-knowledgeable driver for anything beyond Mayfair and Knightsbridge, which are best crossed on foot.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Coverage is excellent; an eSIM (EE or Vodafone) activates before landing, and every good hotel has fast wifi.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Pound sterling; cards and Apple Pay are accepted everywhere and contactless is the norm, so cash is rarely needed; a discretionary 12.5 percent service charge is usually already on restaurant bills.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: May-June and September are kindest: long light, mild days, gardens at their best. Skip November-January for short grey days and persistent damp; August is fine but crowded.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Nonstop from Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru, roughly 9-10 hours. Air India, British Airways and Virgin Atlantic all fly it in a strong business/first cabin; BA First is the standout for through-London itineraries. Ask for arrival into Heathrow T5 and use the Concorde Room if flying BA First.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required; routine boosters only. Very safe; ordinary big-city care with valuables. Tap water is potable throughout.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Effortless for vegetarian and Jain travellers, and Indian food is arguably better than in most Indian cities. Michelin-starred Gymkhana and the Jain-friendly kitchens of Kutir and Trishna are genuinely excellent; pure-veg options abound in Wembley and Southall.
